chapterNote: Chapter 20 is a string of single-verse proverbs, but two threads run through it. The first is the LORD's all-seeing sovereignty over what men cannot see in themselves: He hates the rigged scale (vv. 10, 23), He alone made the eye and ear (v. 12), He searches the depths of a man with His own lamp (v. 27), and He directs the steps no man can chart (v. 24). The second is the king as His earthly image — terrifying as a lion (v. 2), winnowing out evil with his eyes (v. 8) and his threshing wheel (v. 26), kept safe by steadfast love (v. 28). Between these poles the chapter exposes the heart's self-deception: no one can claim a clean heart (v. 9), the buyer lies about the price (v. 14), and the patient must leave vengeance to the LORD who saves (v. 22).

1.text: Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler; whoever staggers under its sway is not wise.
1.amp: Wine [yayin] is a mocker [luts — a scoffer who jeers at restraint], strong drink [shekar] is a brawler [hamah — roaring, turbulent, in an uproar]; whoever is led astray [shagah — made to stagger, reel] by it is not wise [chakam — does not act with skill].
1.notes: luts (H3887) is the same root as the scoffer of 1:22 — drink does not merely loosen a man, it makes him a mocker. hamah (H1993) pictures the roar of a crowd or the surge of the sea; shekar (H7941) is any strong fermented drink. The proverb personifies the bottle as the very company of fools a young man was warned to avoid.

2.text: The dread a king inspires is like the roaring of a lion; whoever stirs him to fury forfeits his own life.
2.amp: The terror [emah — dread, awe] of a king [melek] is like the roaring [naham] of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger [abar — crosses over the line, oversteps] sins against [chata — misses the mark, brings guilt upon] his own soul [nephesh — life, very self].
2.notes: emah (H367) is the dread that falls on prey before the predator; abar (H5674), 'to cross over,' captures the rashness of a man who oversteps the king's bounds. To enrage the sovereign is not a political risk but, the wordplay insists, a chata (H2398) against one's own nephesh (H5315) — a self-wounding sin.

3.text: It is a man's honor to keep clear of strife, but every fool comes charging into a quarrel.
3.amp: It is an honor [kabod — glory, weight, dignity] for a man [ish] to cease [shabath — to desist, leave off] from strife [riyb — a dispute, lawsuit, contention], but every fool [evil — the morally dense fool] will be quarreling [gala — exposes himself, breaks out into it].
3.notes: kabod (H3519) carries the sense of weight — real dignity lies in the heaviness of self-restraint, not in winning the argument. riyb (H7379) is a legal or personal dispute; the evil (H191), the thick-headed fool, cannot leave a fight alone but plunges in, mistaking belligerence for strength.

4.text: The sluggard will not plow when winter comes; so at harvest he looks for a crop and finds nothing.
4.amp: The sluggard [atsel — the lazy man] will not plow [charash] by reason of the cold [choreph — the autumn-into-winter season]; therefore he will beg [shaal — ask, inquire after] at harvest [qatsir], and have nothing.
4.notes: atsel (H6102) is the book's chronic figure of laziness; charash (H2790) can mean both 'to plow' and 'to be silent,' a quiet irony — the man too still to break the ground will later break his silence only to beg. The proverb tracks one missed season into an empty qatsir (H7105): refusal to labor in its time yields nothing in the harvest's time.

5.text: The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a person of understanding draws it up.
5.amp: Counsel [etsah — purpose, plan, design] in the heart [leb] of a man [ish] is like deep [amoq] water; but a man of understanding [tebunah — discernment] will draw it out [dalah — draw up, as from a well].
5.notes: etsah (H6098) is the plan or purpose lying hidden in the leb (H3820); like water at the bottom of a well, it is real but out of reach. dalah (H1802) is the patient labor of lowering a bucket and hauling it up — the discerning person (tebunah, H8394) has the skill to draw out what another keeps buried, whether his own deep motive or his neighbor's.

6.text: Many a man proclaims his own loyal love, but a truly faithful man — who can find him?
6.amp: Most [rob — the multitude] of men [adam] will proclaim [qara — call out, announce] every one his own goodness [chesed — steadfast, loyal love]; but a faithful [emun — trustworthy, reliable] man, who can find [matsa]?
6.notes: chesed (H2617) is covenant loyalty, the love that keeps faith — and everyone advertises his own. The proverb turns on the gap between the claim and the rarity: emun (H529), proven trustworthiness, is the thing actually scarce. The wistful 'who can find?' echoes the search for the rare and precious throughout the book (cf. 31:10).

7.text: The righteous man walks in his integrity; blessed are his children who come after him.
7.amp: The just [tsaddiq — righteous, in right standing] man walks [halak — continually goes, lives] in his integrity [tom — wholeness, blamelessness]; his children [ben] are blessed [esher — happy, well-off] after [achar] him.
7.notes: halak (H1980) in the participle is a settled manner of life, not a single act — the tsaddiq (H6662) lives in his tom (H8537), his unbroken wholeness. The blessing spills past the man himself onto the next generation (esher, H835): integrity is an inheritance, the moral estate a father leaves his ben (H1121).

8.text: A king seated on the throne of judgment winnows out all evil with his eyes.
8.amp: A king [melek] who sits [yashab — is enthroned, presides] on the throne [kisse] of judgment [din — legal verdict] scatters [zarah — winnows, sifts away the chaff] all evil [ra] with his eyes [ayin].
8.notes: zarah (H2219) is the farmer's winnowing — tossing the threshed grain so the wind carries off the chaff; the just king does this to ra (H7451) with a mere look. The din (H1779) throne is the seat of verdict; the verse anticipates v. 26, where the same winnowing image returns with the threshing wheel.

9.text: Who can say, 'I have kept my heart clean; I am pure from my sin'?
9.amp: Who can say [amar], I have made my heart [leb] clean [zakah — purified, made innocent], I am pure [taher — ceremonially and morally clean] from my sin [chattath]?
9.notes: the chapter's quiet hinge: against the all-seeing king (v. 8) and the all-searching LORD (v. 27), no one may claim a cleansed leb (H3820). zakah (H2135) and taher (H2891) are both purity words drawn from the sanctuary, and chattath (H2403) is sin that needs a sin-offering — the unanswerable question exposes universal guilt and points beyond self-cleansing (cf. Ps 51:10; 1 John 1:8).

10.text: A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure — the LORD detests them both alike.
10.amp: Differing weights [even ve-even — literally 'a stone and a stone,' two different stones for weighing] and differing measures [ephah ve-ephah — 'an ephah and an ephah,' two different baskets], both of them are alike an abomination [toevah — a detestable thing] to the LORD [YHWH].
10.notes: the Hebrew idiom 'a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah' (even, H68; ephah, H374) names the cheat's two stones — a heavy one for buying, a light one for selling. toevah (H8441) is the strongest word for what God loathes, usually reserved for idolatry; here it brands the rigged scale, for fraud against a neighbor is sacrilege against the LORD who sees the merchant's pocket (cf. v. 23; Deut 25:13-16).

11.text: Even a child reveals himself by his deeds, whether what he does is pure and upright.
11.amp: Even a child [naar — a boy, youth] is known [nakar — is recognized, gives himself away] by his doings [maalal — his practices], whether his work [poal] is pure [zak — clean, transparent], and whether it is right [yashar — straight, upright].
11.notes: nakar (H5234) means to be recognized or made out — even a naar (H5288) cannot hide his bent; conduct outs character early. zak (H2134) is clean and see-through, yashar (H3477) is straight; the proverb teaches that the moral grain of a life shows in its acts long before its words, and shows even in the young.

12.text: The ear that hears and the eye that sees — the LORD made them both.
12.amp: The hearing [shama — listening] ear [ozen], and the seeing [raah] eye [ayin], the LORD [YHWH] has made [asah] even both of them.
12.notes: shama (H8085) is more than to register sound — it shades into 'to obey'; raah (H7200) likewise into 'to perceive.' Because the LORD asah (H6213) the very organs of perception, He sees and hears what passes through them (cf. Ps 94:9): the verse turns ear and eye from instruments of man's judging into evidence of God's. He who made them is not blind to their use.

13.text: Do not love sleep, or you will come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have your fill of bread.
13.amp: Love [ahab] not sleep [shenah], lest you come to poverty [yarash — be dispossessed, made poor]; open [paqach — open wide] your eyes [ayin], and you will be satisfied [saba — filled, have enough] with bread [lechem].
13.notes: ahab (H157) is the strong word for love and desire — the sluggard does not merely sleep but loves it. paqach (H6491), to open the eyes, plays against the closed eyes of slumber: wakefulness and labor lead to saba (H7646), a full belly of lechem (H3899), where loving sleep leads to dispossession. The bread of v. 13 sets up the deceptive bread of v. 17.

14.text: 'Worthless, worthless!' says the buyer — then off he goes and boasts of his bargain.
14.amp: It is bad [ra], it is bad [ra], says [amar] the buyer [qanah — the one acquiring]; but when he is gone [azal — has departed] his way, then he boasts [halal — praises, congratulates himself].
14.notes: the doubled ra (H7451), 'bad, bad,' is the haggler's patter, running down the goods to drive the price down. The irony is sharp: the same halal (H1984), the verb for praising God, the buyer turns on himself once he has gone (azal, H235) — crowing over the deal he just disparaged. The proverb quietly catalogs the small lies of the marketplace.

15.text: There is gold and a wealth of rubies, but lips that speak knowledge are a jewel beyond price.
15.amp: There is gold [zahab], and a multitude [rob] of rubies [peninim — corals or red jewels]; but the lips [saphah] of knowledge [daat] are a precious [yeqar — rare, costly] jewel [keli — vessel, article of value].
15.notes: the verse weighs treasure against treasure: gold (zahab, H2091) and peninim (H6443) are abundant, but lips that pour out daat (H1847) are the yeqar (H3366), the truly rare keli (H3627). Wisdom recurringly out-prices precious stones (3:15; 8:11); here the rarity is not the knowledge but the mouth disciplined to speak it well.

16.text: Take the garment of one who gives surety for a stranger; hold it in pledge when he stands surety for foreigners.
16.amp: Take [laqach — seize, take in hand] the garment [beged] of him who is surety [arab — pledges himself, guarantees a debt] for a stranger [zur — an outsider]; and take a pledge [chabal] of him for a foreign woman [nokri].
16.notes: the proverb is a hard-nosed credit rule: laqach (H3947) the beged (H899) — the outer cloak that was a man's blanket and security — from anyone reckless enough to arab (H6148), to guarantee an outsider's debt. If he will not protect himself, demand collateral from him. beged also means 'treachery,' a fitting overtone for the tangle that rash surety creates (cf. 6:1-5; 11:15).

17.text: Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth is full of gravel.
17.amp: Bread [lechem] of deceit [sheqer — falsehood, fraud] is sweet [arev — pleasant] to a man [ish]; but afterward [achar] his mouth [peh] shall be filled [male] with gravel [chatsats — grit, small stones].
17.notes: lechem (H3899) won by sheqer (H8267), the bread of fraud, is arev (H6149), sweet on the tongue — sin's pleasure is real but momentary. The reversal is visceral: the same peh (H6310) that savored it grinds on chatsats (H2687), gravel, when the reckoning comes. Ill-gotten gain turns to grit; the appetite outlasts the sweetness (cf. v. 13's honest bread).

18.text: Plans take firm shape by counsel; so wage your war only with wise guidance.
18.amp: Every purpose [machashabah — plan, scheme, thought] is established [kun — made firm, set fast] by counsel [etsah]; and with wise guidance [tachbuloth — steerings, sound strategy] make [asah] war [milchamah].
18.notes: machashabah (H4284) is the plan in the mind; only etsah (H6098), taken counsel, makes it kun (H3559), firm. tachbuloth (H8458) comes from the word for a ship's ropes — the wisdom that steers (cf. 1:5) — and the proverb applies it to milchamah (H4421): even war, the gravest venture, must be steered by counsel rather than driven by impulse.

19.text: A gossip betrays confidences; so keep no company with the man who talks too freely.
19.amp: He who goes about [halak] as a talebearer [rakil — a slanderer, peddler of gossip] reveals [galah — uncovers, lays bare] secrets [sod — private counsel, intimate confidence]; therefore do not associate [arab — mingle, keep company] with him who flatters [pathah — entices, persuades] with his lips [saphah].
19.notes: the rakil (H7400) traffics in galah (H1540) of the sod (H5475) — exposing the intimate counsel of a trusting circle. The warning sharpens by wordplay: arab (H6148), 'do not mix' with him, is the very surety-word of v. 16, here 'entangle yourself'; the man whose lips pathah (H6601), open wide to flatter and entice, will as easily open them to spill your secrets.

20.text: Whoever curses his father or mother — his lamp will be snuffed out in deepest darkness.
20.amp: Whoever curses [qalal — treats with contempt, makes light of] his father [av] or his mother [em], his lamp [ner] shall be put out [daak — extinguished] in blackest [ishon — the deep pupil of the eye, utter] darkness [choshek].
20.notes: qalal (H7043), literally 'to make light,' is the opposite of honoring (kabad, 'to make weighty') one's parents — to belittle father or mother is to break the commandment with the heaviest weight (cf. Exod 21:17). The ner (H5216), the household lamp, signifies a man's life and continuing line; daak (H1846) snuffs it out in ishon choshek (H380 + H2822), the pitch-black at the eye's center — no light, no future.

21.text: An inheritance grabbed in greedy haste at the start will not be blessed in the end.
21.amp: An inheritance [nachalah — heritage, possession] gotten hastily [bahal — seized in rash haste / bachal — gotten by greed] at the beginning [rishon]; but the end [acharith — the latter outcome] of it shall not be blessed [barak].
21.notes: the textual tradition hears two roots in the verb — bahal (H926), to grab in panicked haste, and bachal (H973), to grasp greedily — and both fit: a nachalah (H5159) snatched at the rishon (H7223), the front end, by impatience or greed. The proverb sets the grasping start against the acharith (H319), the end God weighs; what is seized without blessing cannot end in barak (H1288).

22.text: Do not say, 'I will pay back this wrong.' Wait for the LORD, and He will deliver you.
22.amp: Say [amar] not, I will repay [shalam — requite, settle the score] evil [ra]; wait [qavah — wait expectantly, hope] for the LORD [YHWH], and He shall save [yasha — deliver, rescue] you.
22.notes: shalam (H7999), built on the root of shalom, ordinarily means to make whole or pay what is due — the tempting logic of personal vengeance dressed up as 'settling accounts.' The proverb forbids it and substitutes qavah (H6960), the taut, hopeful waiting on YHWH, who alone will yasha (H3467). Vengeance is surrendered upward (cf. Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19).

23.text: A weight and a weight the LORD detests, and dishonest scales are not good.
23.amp: Differing weights [even ve-even — 'a stone and a stone'] are an abomination [toevah] to the LORD [YHWH]; and a false [mirmah — deceitful] balance [mozen — scales] is not good [tov].
23.notes: a near-twin of v. 10, framing the chapter's market-fraud theme: again the two stones (even, H68) are a toevah (H8441) to the LORD. mirmah (H4820) is treachery, and the litotes 'not good' (lo tov) understates with biting restraint — the rigged mozen (H3976) is not merely imperfect but loathsome to God, who watches every transaction (cf. v. 12).

24.text: A man's steps are directed by the LORD; how then can anyone understand his own way?
24.amp: Man's [geber — a strong man, warrior] goings [mitsad — steps, footsteps] are of the LORD [YHWH]; how can a man [adam] then understand [biyn — discern, make sense of] his own way [derek]?
24.notes: even the geber (H1397), the man at the height of his powers, does not master his own mitsad (H4703) — the LORD orders the steps (cf. 16:9; Jer 10:23). The question is humbling: if the very footfalls are appointed from above, how can frail adam (H120) fully biyn (H995) his own derek (H1870)? Wisdom ends in trust, not in self-charted certainty.

25.text: It is a snare to vow rashly, 'This is holy!' and only afterward to weigh the vows.
25.amp: It is a snare [moqesh — a trap, bait] to a man [adam] who devours [yala — rashly swallows, blurts out] that which is holy [qodesh — a dedicated, sacred thing], and after [achar] vows [neder — a binding pledge] to make inquiry [baqar — to consider, reconsider].
25.notes: the moqesh (H4170) is the trap of the hasty tongue in worship: to yala (H3216) — to gulp out, blurt — the word qodesh (H6944), rashly dedicating something to God, and only achar (H310), afterward, to baqar (H1239), weigh whether the neder (H5088) can be kept. Vows to God are not to be flung out and then second-guessed (cf. Eccl 5:4-5; Judg 11:30-35).

26.text: A wise king winnows out the wicked and drives the threshing wheel over them.
26.amp: A wise [chakam — skilled, discerning] king [melek] scatters [zarah — winnows] the wicked [rasha], and brings [shub — turns, drives back] the wheel [ophan — the threshing wheel] over them.
26.notes: zarah (H2219) returns from v. 8 — the chakam (H2450) king sifts the rasha (H7563) like chaff; then the agricultural image hardens as he drives the ophan (H212), the studded threshing wheel, over them to crush the grain from the husk. Justice is portrayed as a harvest process: separation first, then the crushing weight of the verdict.

27.text: The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out all his innermost being.
27.amp: The spirit [neshamah — breath, breath of life] of man [adam] is the candle [ner — lamp] of the LORD [YHWH], searching [chaphas — searching out, examining] all the inward parts [cheder — inner chambers] of the belly [beten — the innermost being].
27.notes: neshamah (H5397) is the breath of life God breathed into Adam (Gen 2:7) — and that very life-breath He uses as His ner (H5216), a lamp lowered into the dark chambers of the self. chaphas (H2664) is to ransack and search out; the LORD probes the chadrei-beten (H2315 + H990), the deepest inner rooms, answering v. 9: no heart is hidden from the One who lit the searching flame within it.

28.text: Loyal love and faithfulness keep a king safe; by steadfast love his throne is upheld.
28.amp: Mercy [chesed — steadfast, covenant love] and truth [emeth — faithfulness, reliability] preserve [natsar — guard, watch over] the king [melek]; and his throne [kisse] is upheld [saad — supported, sustained] by mercy [chesed].
28.notes: the king who terrifies (v. 2) and winnows (vv. 8, 26) is himself kept by softer powers: chesed (H2617) and emeth (H571) — the paired covenant virtues of God Himself (Exod 34:6) — natsar (H5341) him as sentries. saad (H5582) is to prop and sustain; a throne does not finally stand on fear but on steadfast love, the very quality that secures God's own rule.

29.text: The glory of young men is their strength; the splendor of old men is their gray head.
29.amp: The glory [tipheret — beauty, splendor] of young men [bachur — youths in their prime] is their strength [koach]; and the beauty [hadar — majesty, honor] of old men [zaqen — elders] is the gray head [seyvah].
29.notes: the proverb honors both seasons without rivalry: the tipheret (H8597) of the bachur (H970) is raw koach (H3581), vigor in its prime; the hadar (H1926) of the zaqen (H2205) is the seyvah (H7872), the crown of gray won by years (cf. 16:31). Strength and age each have their proper splendor; wisdom values the one without despising the other.

30.text: Bruising blows scour away evil, and beatings reach the innermost being.
30.amp: The blueness [chaburah — the welt, the bruise of a wound] of a wound [petsa — a gash, stripe] cleanses away [maraq — scours, purges] evil [ra]; so do stripes [makkah — blows, beatings] the inward parts [cheder — inner chambers] of the belly [beten — the innermost being].
30.notes: chaburah (H2250) is the dark welt a blow raises; the marginal Hebrew reads it as a purging medicine that maraq (H8562) — scours — away ra (H7451). The hard truth is that painful discipline, the makkah (H4347) that reaches the chadrei-beten (H2315 + H990), can cleanse where gentler means fail. The same inner chambers the LORD searches in v. 27 are here scrubbed clean by correction (cf. Heb 12:11).
